english: Sirmio, bright eye of every peninsula and island, I am home. The lake laughs under the wind the way it did when I was a boy, and I set down the pack of Bithynia on the doorstep. Let us live, old friend, and count the kisses again until the counting itself is lost; the short light goes down once and the night is one unbroken sleep. Be stubborn, heart, and do not run after what runs away; the girl who shone for me is shining for someone else. Now spring brings back the warm days and the sky is no longer hoarse with storms; the mind itches to travel and the feet grow glad. Through many nations and many seas I came to my brother's grave to say what the dust cannot answer: hail and farewell, for ever.

answer:
I'll check each suspected echo against the corpus (concordance lines, headword use, forms) and scan the Catullan lines for the phalaecian.Next I need the headword evidence (la_lemma) and scansions: the Catullan lines in phalaecian, and the choliambic/elegiac lines tested against the same template.Two re-set fragments from 101 to check (the pentameter can't go in whole), then I'll answer.Five Catullan poems, in the order the English runs. Evidence is from la_forms / la_lemma / la_concordance; the metre verdicts are the lint bank's (template `xx-uu-u-u-F`).

**1. Sirmio … bright eye … I am home → c. 31 (choliambic)**
- *Paene insularum, Sirmio, insularumque / ocelle* (31.1–2). `Sirmio` 2 tokens, both in 31 and both elided; `ocelle` 2 tokens (31.2, 50.19), headword *ocellus* 7× in Catullus (*ocellis* 43, *ocellos* 45, *ocelli* 3).
- "the lake laughs": *ridete, quidquid est domi cachinnorum* (31.14); *cachinnus* 4× (31, 13, 56, 64.273 of waves).
- "I am home / set down the pack": 31.7–9 *cum mens onus reponit … venimus larem ad nostrum*; *salve, o venusta Sirmio* (31.12). "Bithynia": 31.5 *Thyniam atque Bithynos*; the word *Bithynia* itself is in a phalaecian, 10.7 *iam Bithynia, quo modo se haberet*.
- Phalaecian reuse: the choliambic line will not go in whole (pos. 2 of *insularum* is short where the base wants a long; scanner confirms a mis-fit). Fragments that do sit: *ocelle* ⏑–⏑ (pos. 5–7 or 7–9), *insularum ocelle* at 6–11 with the -um elided, *venusta Sirmio* at 5–10, *Bithynia* ⏑–⏑⏑. Four re-settings passed and are on your screen (*salve, Sirmio, et insularum ocelle* etc.); note the two with unelided *Sirmiō* have no Catullan evidence for the quantity.

**2. Let us live … count the kisses … short light … one unbroken sleep → c. 5 (phalaecian)**
- *Vivamus, mea Lesbia, atque amemus* (5.1); *da mi basia mille, deinde centum* (5.7; *basia* 3×, *basiorum* 2×); *conturbabimus illa, ne sciamus* (5.11); *nobis cum semel occidit brevis lux, / nox est perpetua una dormienda* (5.5–6; *perpetua* only here, *perpetuum* 2× in 101).
- Reusable whole: all five lines pass the metre and form checks as complete hendecasyllables (the lint flags them as verbatim "homage", non-blocking). *da mi basia mille* alone fills positions 1–7 exactly. "old friend" replaces *mea Lesbia* (⏑–⏑⏑–): you'll need a vocative of the same shape.

**3. Be stubborn, heart … do not run after what runs away … the girl who shone → c. 8 (choliambic)**
- *nec quae fugit sectare, nec miser vive, / sed obstinata mente perfer, obdura* (8.10–11); *at tu, Catulle, destinatus obdura* (8.19); *obduro* 3× in Catullus (*obdura* ×2, *obdurat* 8.12), once in Horace. *fulsere quondam candidi tibi soles* (8.3, repeated 8.8 with *vere*); *fulgeo* 6× in Catullus.
- Phalaecian reuse: none of these lines fits whole, and *candidi tibi soles* (–⏑⏑⏑⏑––) fits nowhere in the line. Fragments: *obdura* ––⏑ at positions 2–4; *fulsere* ––⏑ likewise at 2–4; *soles candidi* ––-⏑⏑ at 1–5. (Secondary echo for "shining for someone else": 58 *Lesbia nostra … nunc in quadriviis*, which is phalaecian.)

**4. Now spring brings back the warm days … sky no longer hoarse … mind itches … feet grow glad → c. 46 (phalaecian)**
- *Iam ver egelidos refert tepores* (46.1), *iam caeli furor aequinoctialis* (46.2), *iam mens praetrepidans avet vagari* (46.7), *iam laeti studio pedes vigescunt* (46.8). *egelidos*, *tepores*, *praetrepidans*, *vigescunt* are each a single Catullan token (hapax-ish; *tepor* once more in Horace).
- Reusable whole: 46.1, 46.7, 46.8 all pass as complete lines. Your "no longer hoarse with storms" is a paraphrase of 46.2–3 (*furor … silescit*), which would need its own line.

**5. Through many nations and many seas … brother's grave … hail and farewell for ever → c. 101 (elegiac)**
- *Multas per gentes et multa per aequora vectus / advenio has miseras, frater, ad inferias* (101.1–2; *aequora* 4× in Catullus, *inferias* 2×); *mutam nequiquam alloquerer cinerem* (101.4); *atque in perpetuum, frater, ave atque vale* (101.10; *ave* is the only token of that form).
- Phalaecian reuse: hexameter and pentameter can't go in whole; *multa per aequora* fails at position 8 (short *-ra*). What does fit: *in perpetuum* ––⏑⏑– at 2–6, *atque vale* –⏑⏑– at 3–6, and *frater* as the line's cadence. Two re-settings pass the whole bank: *nunc in perpetuum valeque, frater* and *ave in perpetuum valeque, frater* (the latter with iambic base ⏑–, which Catullus allows, cf. 2.4, 3.17; *valeque* is enclitic-formed, not printed by him).

Not Catullan: "the dust cannot answer" is your gloss on 101.4's *mutam … cinerem*; "every peninsula" condenses *paene insularum*.
